evidence_note: Same survey: cobalt-60 units reported, all in clinical use. "They reported 11 megavoltage units in total (seven linear accelerators [LINACs] and four Cobalt-60s) and 10 brachytherapy afterloaders."
Same SAGE Open Medicine survey: functional cobalt-60 machines across the 9 centres. "two Cobalt-60 machines, four Linear Accelerators (LINACs), and three brachytherapy machines"

Same JCO Global Oncology review: cobalt-60 machines as of June 2023 (functional status not stated). "Presently, as of June 2023, there are a total of 14 LINACs, four Cobalt-60 machines, and eight HDR brachytherapy afterloaders available in the country"

Survey of radiation oncologists at Nigeria's radiotherapy centres (data collected around early 2020): linacs in clinical use, out of 7 reported. "Of those, 57% (4/7) of the LINACs, 100% (4/4) of the Cobalt-60s, and 63% (7/11) of the afterloaders were in clinical use."

Same survey: linacs reported but not in clinical use (7 reported minus 4 in use). The paper ties public machine downtime to unfunded maintenance and repair. "Radiotherapy (RT) treatment at public hospitals in Nigeria is often interrupted by prolonged periods of machine breakdown because of insufficient funds for maintenance and repair."

Same SAGE Open Medicine survey: functional megavoltage equipment across the 9 centres (4 linacs and 2 cobalt-60). "only less than 50% of the centers had functional equipment, which include two Cobalt-60 machines, four Linear Accelerators (LINACs), and three brachytherapy machines."

JCO Global Oncology review (Jan 2024), status as of June 2023: linacs in the country. The paper calls them 'working' in one place and 'available' in another, and warns their functionality 'remains unstable'. "Nigeria documents 72 clinical and radiation oncologists practicing in the country (Fig 1 ), 14 working LINACs, and 14 radiation treatment facilities spread across 12 states"

Annals of Medicine and Surgery editorial (2025) summarising a 2021 multicentre study of the 8 government-funded radiotherapy centres: functional linacs out of 7. "Of seven LINACs, only three are functional, and four centers lack any operational teletherapy machines."

ARCON press briefing reported by The Guardian (2022): upper bound on oncologists treating cancer nationally. "Nigeria has less than 100 oncologists providing cancer treatment to over 200 million people."

ARCON's need estimate from the IAEA ratio of one oncologist per 100,000 people (a need, not a count). "countries are supposed to have one oncologist to 100,000 population but in Nigeria, less than 100, oncologists are providing treatment for a population of over 200 million instead of at least 2500 oncologists."

Same SAGE Open Medicine paper: radiation oncologists in Nigeria (with 34 radiation therapists and 31 medical physicists). "There are presently 28 radiation oncologists and 34 radiation therapists in Nigeria"

Same JCO Global Oncology review: clinical and radiation oncologists practising in Nigeria at the time of the review (2023). "Nigeria documents 72 clinical and radiation oncologists practicing in the country"

ARCON president Dr Nwamaka Lasebikan, in her own post reproduced by OncoDaily: upper bound on specialist radiation and clinical oncologists (the figure is 'fewer than 100'). "Nigeria currently has fewer than 100 specialist radiation and clinical oncologists"

Same editorial, citing the 2021 multicentre study of the 8 government-funded centres: radiation oncologists (with 45 residents and 44 medical physicists). "the country has 44 radiation oncologists, 45 residents, 44 medical physicists, and limited other RT personnel, but no medical physics residency programs."

Nigerian Cancer Society president: upper bound on the number of clinical oncologists nationally (the figure is 'fewer than 70'). "Nigeria currently has fewer than 70 clinical oncologists nationwide, which is far below acceptable global standards."

Patient survey at University College Hospital Ibadan (January 2016): radiotherapy centres with working machines at the time, out of 8 centres (1 private, 7 public). "As of January 2016, there were eight radiotherapy centers in Nigeria, one private center and seven public centers" ... "During the time of the study, only two centers had functioning radiotherapy machines."

JCO Global Oncology PPP survey (2021) quoting the then-published IAEA DIRAC directory for Nigeria: centres and megavoltage machines listed (7 each), which the authors say undercounts. "the currently published DIrectory of RAdiotherapy Centres (DIRAC) reports seven existing RT centers and seven megavoltage machines, whereas our findings indicate 12 centers with 12 megavoltage units."

Same JCO Global Oncology survey: the authors' own count of megavoltage units across 12 radiotherapy centres (includes one private linac commissioned after data collection). "our findings indicate 12 centers with 12 megavoltage units."

IAEA authors' analysis of the DIRAC database (Lancet Oncology, 2021): megavoltage units (linacs plus cobalt-60) listed for Nigeria in 2020. DIRAC is self-reported and counts installed units, not proven working ones. Table 3 row: "Nigeria 115 950 122 728 10 0·08 157 165 466 211" under the header "Supply of megavoltage units (2020)"

Same Lancet Oncology/DIRAC paper: megavoltage units needed for Nigeria's 2020 cancer cases (a need estimate assuming 500 patients per machine per year). Table 3 column "Demand for megavoltage units (2020)" gives 157 for Nigeria; text adds "The need in western Africa is concentrated in Nigeria (147 additional megavoltage units needed)"
Same Lancet Oncology/DIRAC paper: megavoltage units needed for projected 2030 cancer cases in Nigeria (165,466 cases). Table 3 column "Demand for megavoltage units (2030)" gives 211 for Nigeria.

In February 2022 an ABUTH oncologist said NHA had the only working external-beam radiotherapy machine in all of northern Nigeria. "no single functional external beam radiotherapy machine in the whole of northern Nigeria" (with the National Hospital Abuja as the exception) [Curation: a regional figure (northern Nigeria), stored under National]

Same ARCON 2022 briefing as reported by Leadership: the speaker narrows 'less than 20' down to about 10 truly functional machines. "presently in Nigeria we still have less than 20 that are functional and as a matter of fact, even when you talk about functionality, we probably have about 10 or so"

ARCON Secretary General Dr Oladele Kehinde (2022): upper bound on functional radiotherapy machines of any type (the figure is 'less than 20'). "Nigeria has less than 20 functional radiotherapy machines."

Then Nigerian Cancer Society president Dr Adamu Umar (Nov 2022): all radiotherapy machines in the country, with most government ones said to be non-functional. "According to Umar, the country has only 13 radiotherapy machines for its teeming population, and most of the machines in government healthcare facilities are not functional."

The Guardian (World Cancer Day 2023): functional radiotherapy machines nationally, per medical experts interviewed. "Currently, Nigeria has four functional radiotherapy machines serving over 200 million persons across the 36 states and Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja"

SAGE Open Medicine survey (data May 2020 to April 2021) of 9 radiotherapy centres: centres with at least one functional piece of equipment. "Out of nine centers evaluated, only four had at least one functional equipment"

Report of the IARC 2025 assessment: 15 working machines in 8 states (Lagos, Enugu, Ebonyi, Cross River, Borno, Abuja, Kano, Sokoto), against a need of over 120. Power cuts and missing maintenance contracts are named as causes. No facility-level breakdown is given. "Nigeria has only 15 functional radiotherapy machines distributed across eight states"; "lack of maintenance contracts particularly in facilities outside the public-private partnerships framework"

Same IARC assessment as quoted by BusinessDay: number of radiotherapy machines needed nationally (a need estimate, not a count of existing machines). "The country would require over 120 radiotherapy machines to adequately treat all cancer patients"

President of the Nigerian Cancer Society (Abidemi Omonisi), in a Daily Trust interview: functional radiotherapy machines nationally, public and private combined. "At present, we have a minimum of about ten functional radiotherapy machines actively working across the country, including those in both public and private facilities."

GLOBOCAN 2022 estimate of new cancer cases in Nigeria (both sexes, all ages), as quoted by BusinessDay. The IARC fact sheet now online shows the newer GLOBOCAN 2024 edition, so the 2022 figure was confirmed only through this secondary source. "According to IARC Globocan, in 2022, Nigeria recorded approximately 127,763 new cancer cases (48,096 in men and 79,667 in women)"
GLOBOCAN 2022 estimate of cancer deaths in Nigeria, as quoted by BusinessDay (same caveat as the case count). "and 79,542 cancer deaths (32,905 in men and 46,637 in women)"

A 2026 report citing a Nigerian Cancer Society assessment: about ten working machines nationally. Only 2 of 8 government-funded centres treat patients consistently, and the article blames erratic power, poor maintenance and no residency training for medical physicists. "Nigeria has barely ten functional radiotherapy machines for a population exceeding 200 million"

IARC Global Cancer Observatory fact sheet for Nigeria, GLOBOCAN 2024 edition (released September 2026): estimated new cancer cases in 2024, both sexes. This newer estimate supersedes the GLOBOCAN 2022 figure. Fact sheet headline reads "Statistics at a glance, 2024" with "Number of new cases" shown as 152 261.
Same GLOBOCAN 2024 fact sheet: estimated cancer deaths in Nigeria in 2024, both sexes (5-year prevalent cases: 292,934). Fact sheet headline "Number of deaths" shown as 90 795.

Secondary news feature (Modern Ghana, Nov 2026) attributing to unnamed 'stakeholders' a count of operational linacs and licensed practitioners; not traced to a primary source. "Stakeholders noted that fewer than 80 licensed radiotherapy practitioners serve about 12 operational linear accelerators across the country."
